findings.consequence: Any superuser or global-access member who requests the audit log with optimized_pagination=true and gets at least one row receives a 500 error. A crafted cursor with a negative offset also causes a 500.
findings.explanation: The kwarg is forwarded fine (paginate takes **paginator_kwargs and OptimizedCursorPaginator.__init__ accepts enable_advanced_features). But OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key (paginator.py:838-840) calls math.floor/ceil directly on getattr(item, "datetime"), a datetime object, whereas DateTimePaginator converts it to a timestamp first. Any non-empty page raises TypeError when the cursor is built. value_from_cursor also returns the raw numeric cursor value instead of converting it to a datetime, so cursor-based filtering on the datetime column is wrong. In addition, the enable_advanced_features path slices the queryset with a user-supplied negative cursor offset, which Django rejects (AssertionError, 500), and the code comment about accessing data beyond normal bounds is misleading.
findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator used on datetime field crashes; negative offsets also exposed

findings.consequence: A request to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor such as "0:-1:0" returns an unhandled 500 error. Only superusers and members with global access can reach the path. If a backend ever honored negative slices, the same path would bypass the pagination bounds.
findings.explanation: Cursor.from_string (src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:53-61) accepts any int for the offset, including negative values, and nothing else clamps it. With optimized_pagination=true and an admin user, the endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True. In get_result, a cursor with offset < 0 takes the new branch, which runs queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise AssertionError("Negative indexing is not supported."). The comment claiming Django handles negative slicing is wrong. The normal branch clamps the offset with max(0, offset), and this branch drops that clamp. For a cursor like "0:-5:0", stop = -5 + limit + 1 is also negative, so it fails the same way.
findings.title: Negative cursor offset is sliced directly on the queryset, causing a 500 error

findings.consequence: Malformed forward cursors now return page one instead of an error. The comment misleads readers about what the code does.
findings.explanation: The change adds `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. A forward cursor with a negative offset used to be passed straight to the queryset slice. Now it is silently clamped to 0, so it returns the first page, while the later `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check still uses the unclamped offset. The comment says negative offsets are allowed, but the code clamps them (except for prev cursors, where they still reach the slice unchanged). This alters behavior for every BasePaginator subclass without being needed for the new feature.
findings.title: BasePaginator.get_result now clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors, and its comment claims the opposite

findings.consequence: Any client can send a crafted prev cursor with a negative offset and trigger an unhandled exception (HTTP 500) on every endpoint that uses BasePaginator. Prev pagination can also return the wrong rows.
findings.explanation: The change sets `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For prev cursors the raw offset is used in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. The Cursor constructor in src/sentry/utils/cursors.py:28 accepts any int, including negative ones, and the cursor string comes from the request. A prev cursor such as `0:-5:1` therefore produces a negative slice start. Django querysets reject negative indexing with an AssertionError, which becomes a 500. Even when `stop` is positive, a negative start is not a valid row offset. The comment claiming the queryset handles boundary conditions is wrong. The original code never clamped, but the old code had no stated support for negative offsets either. This change now deliberately lets them through for all BasePaginator subclasses. The `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` check at line 192 also still uses the unclamped offset.
findings.title: Negative offset is passed through to the queryset slice for prev cursors

findings.consequence: A crafted or corrupted prev cursor with a negative offset makes any endpoint using BasePaginator raise an unhandled error (HTTP 500), or return wrong rows. Before the change the offset was used unmodified for forward cursors and the same applied for prev, but negative values are now explicitly endorsed, and forward cursors are clamped inconsistently with prev.
findings.explanation: The change sets `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. Prev cursors therefore pass a raw, possibly negative offset into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. The offset comes from the client-supplied cursor string, and `Cursor.__init__` only does `int(offset)`; its comment says negative offsets are allowed. A cursor like `0:-5:1` gives a negative slice start. Django QuerySets reject negative indexing with an AssertionError ("Negative indexing is not supported."). Non-QuerySet paginators, such as list-based ones, would instead slice from the end of the list and return wrong rows. The comment's claim that the queryset handles boundary conditions is false. findings.title: Negative offset now reaches queryset slicing for prev cursors

findings.consequence: For allowlisted projects, the stats endpoint can run a `sum(sample_weight)` aggregation on a dataset that has no such column, which fails the request. In other cases error counts are silently left unscaled.
findings.explanation: _get_event_stats takes a `scoped_dataset` parameter and runs the query against it. The eligibility check, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, is passed the closed-over outer `dataset` instead. The dashboard split-discover path calls _get_event_stats with `discover`, `errors` or `transactions` as `scoped_dataset` (around lines 346-400 and 488). So the check judges a different dataset from the one queried. If the request dataset is discover and the query goes to transactions, the check judges discover, which can return True from `event.type:error` in the query string. Then `upsampled_count()`, which sums `sample_weight`, is run against transactions. If the request dataset is transactions or another dataset and the split runs against errors, upsampling is wrongly skipped.
findings.title: Upsampling eligibility uses outer `dataset` instead of `scoped_dataset`

findings.consequence: After the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option changes, every cached project set keeps its old eligibility for up to 60 seconds. Queries can return upsampled counts for projects that were just removed, or raw counts for projects that were just added. On a hash collision, a non-allowlisted project set could get another set's eligibility. The collision is unlikely in practice. Th…
findings.explanation: The cache key at line 27 is built from `hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids)))`, so it holds a 64-bit digest and not the ids. Two different project sets in the same org that hash to the same value share one cache entry. The second set would then get the first set's eligibility decision. The ids themselves would make a collision-free key. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (lines 67-74) rebuilds the same hashed key. A grep finds no caller anywhere in the snapshot, and no option-change hook calls it. It can only delete the entry for one exact project set, so it could not invalidate every set affected by an allowlist change even if it were called.
findings.title: Eligibility cache key uses hash() of project ids and the invalidation helper is never called

findings.consequence: Allowlisted projects get silently unscaled counts for aliased or parameterised count columns, and the response keys can change.
findings.explanation: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites a column only when it equals `count()` after lower-casing and stripping. Columns such as `count() as x` or `count(id)` are left unchanged, so they stay unscaled. The result is also inconsistent: in the same request, a plain `count()` is upsampled and other count forms are not. The rewrite also forces the alias `count`. A request with a different alias, or with both `count()` and another column, can change the response key names.
findings.title: Transform only matches the exact string `count()`

findings.consequence: A user can request `upsampled_count()` on a non-allowlisted project or on the transactions dataset. The query fails with a Snuba error instead of returning a validation error. It also adds a new public query function that becomes part of the API surface.
findings.explanation: The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added without `private=True`, unlike the neighbouring internal `column_hash`. It is therefore a user-callable aggregate in the Discover query language. Its snql is `sum(sample_weight)`. The code's own comments say this column exists only for events in allowlisted error projects. The same function converter is used for transactions and other non-allowlisted queries. A user who requests `upsampled_count()` on such a query makes Snuba reference a column that is missing or unqualified. Nothing in the changed code guards this (the eligibility check in error_upsampling.py is only applied by the helper's callers, and the grep found no caller).
findings.title: upsampled_count is registered as a public Discover function that depends on a column that may not exist

findings.consequence: An attacker can use login CSRF to bind their own GitHub identity to the victim's integration setup. That defeats the purpose of the OAuth step, which is to prove that the installing user controls the GitHub account.
findings.explanation: OAuthLoginView uses `pipeline.signature` as the OAuth `state` and later checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. In src/sentry/pipeline/base.py:132-133 the signature is `md5(module.ClassName of each pipeline view)`. It is identical for every user, session and run, and it is not secret. It is not a per-flow random nonce. The comparison is also not constant-time, but that matters much less. An attacker can authorize the GitHub app with their own account and get a `code`. They then send the victim a link to the setup URL with `?state=<known constant>&code=<attacker code>`. If the victim has a GitHub pipeline in progress in their session, the check passes. The code is exchanged and the attacker's GitHub login is stored as `github_authenticated_user`. The `code` is also not tied to the flow that started it.
findings.title: OAuth state is a static, public value, so it gives no CSRF protection

findings.consequence: If GitHub is slow or unreachable, or the user-info call returns 401, 403 or 5xx, the GitHub integration setup returns an unhandled 500 instead of the intended error page. The user cannot complete the installation and sees a crash.
findings.explanation: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(...)` at line 423 is called outside the `try`. `safe_urlopen` in src/sentry/http.py calls `session.request(...)` with a 30s timeout and does not catch anything. A connection error, timeout or blocked-IP error from the requests library therefore escapes the view. The `try` only covers decoding the body. `get_user_info(payload['access_token'])` at line 434 calls `resp.raise_for_status()` in src/sentry/identity/github/provider.py. It raises `HTTPError` on any non-2xx response, for example a revoked or invalid token. It can also raise network exceptions. Nothing in the view catches these, although the view already has an `error(...)` path for failed auth.
findings.title: GitHub OAuth token exchange and user lookup are not wrapped in error handling

findings.consequence: A user can link another account's GitHub App installation, one not yet in Sentry, to their own Sentry organization. This is the hijack the OAuth step was added to stop. Integrations created before this change that lack `sender` metadata will return a 500 instead of the error page.
findings.explanation: GitHubInstallation.dispatch takes installation_id from request.GET first, so a request in the install step can override the value bound earlier. If no Integration row exists for that id, the `except Integration.DoesNotExist` branch calls `pipeline.next_step()` straight away. The `github_authenticated_user` versus `metadata['sender']['login']` comparison sits only on the later path, where an Integration already exists. A user who has finished the OAuth step as themselves can therefore send `installation_id=<someone else's installation>` and skip the ownership check. The only remaining check is in build_integration, which just confirms the installation exists. Separately, `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` (line 503) raises KeyError for legacy integrations that have no `sender` metadata.
findings.title: GitHub user check is skipped when no Integration exists for the installation_id

findings.consequence: The test can pass even if the 404 handling for a missing GitHub installation is broken or removed. The not-found behavior it is named for is no longer verified.
findings.explanation: The test never starts the pipeline: it has no init_path request. It then sends a code/state pair with state "ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05". Every other updated test uses the pipeline state "9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3". The assertion was changed from "The GitHub installation could not be found." to the generic "Invalid installation request.". That message is most likely produced by the missing or mismatched pipeline state, before the stubbed 404 on /app/installations/<id> is ever reached. I did not trace the view code to confirm the source of the message.

findings.consequence: Malformed reports that the old code rejected are now accepted with a 200. This only affects the experimental metrics collector, so the impact is small.
findings.explanation: The old BrowserReport dataclass required `timestamp`. In the new BrowserReportSerializer, both `age` and `timestamp` are `required=False`. The cross-field checks run only when a field is present, and they test truthiness of the other field. A report with neither field therefore validates. A report with `age: 0` plus a `timestamp` also passes, because `initial_data.get("age")` is falsy. The comment says exactly one of the two must be present, but the code does not enforce that.

findings.consequence: With any missing or duplicated error event, the error context sent to Seer carries wrong event ids. The summary can then mislabel errors.
findings.explanation: nodestore.get_multi returns a dict keyed by node id. It deduplicates ids and only includes ids it found, so missing events are absent. The code zips error_ids with events.values(). If any error event is missing from nodestore, or an id is duplicated, every later value is paired with the wrong event_id. The `id` field then belongs to a different event. Because the filter `if data is not None` is applied after the zip, it never catches the missing entries, since missing keys are simply absent. The `id` is also not the node id the dict is keyed by.
findings.title: Error IDs mis-paired with nodestore results via zip(error_ids, events.values())

findings.consequence: Seer receives all errors at the start of the log instead of at their position in the timeline. This degrades summary accuracy. Because error_events are passed to every page, the errors are also repeated in each paginated segment page.
findings.explanation: gen_request_data compares error_events[i]["timestamp"], taken from the nodestore event payload, with event.get("timestamp", 0) from the replay recording segments. Nodestore event timestamps are epoch seconds. Replay recording event timestamps are epoch milliseconds. Every error is therefore numerically smaller than every replay event. All errors are emitted before the first replay event, so they are not interleaved chronologically as the docstring promises.
findings.title: Error timestamps (seconds) compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

findings.consequence: In the default view, with no search, the span attributes list still shows is_segment, project_id and received. The list shows these attributes when the search is empty and drops them when the user searches.

With no query, the code returns `sorted` unfiltered, so is_segment, project_id and received are shown. When the user types a query that matches them, they are hidden. The hiding therefore only happens during a search, which is the reverse of the intent.

findings.consequence: After a hang, the old flusher process stays alive and keeps running next to its replacement. Both flush and produce the same shard segments, which duplicates segments in Kafka and leaks processes on every restart. On shutdown, stuck flusher processes are not terminated.
findings.explanation: The flusher builds its processes with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which creates `SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process`, which is what `multiprocessing.Process` refers to. So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for real flusher processes. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Now, in `_ensure_processes_alive` (lines 253-257), a process whose healthy_since timestamp is stale (cause "hang") is not killed. `_create_process_for_shards` then starts a second process on the same shards. The same check in `join()` (line 346) means `process.terminate()` is never called, so a flusher process that is still running after join is not terminated.
findings.title: isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

findings.consequence: The `queued` timestamp is wrong for every assignment source. It is the worker's import time, not the enqueue time, and gets older the longer the process runs. Any logic that relies on it gets incorrect results.
findings.explanation: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated when the class body runs, at module import. Every AssignmentSource built through from_integration (sync.py lines 98 and 115) gets the same process-start timestamp as `queued`, not the time it was created. to_dict then sends that stale value to the Celery task. If anything uses `queued` to order or dedupe assignment events, it will see wrong values. The field needs `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

findings.consequence: For an affected partition, the committed offset stops advancing and the tracked offsets accumulate in memory. After a restart or rebalance the consumer reprocesses everything since the stall, and consumer lag is reported as growing.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets walks range(start, max_offset+1) and breaks at the first offset that is not in all_offsets. After mark_committed, start becomes last_committed+1. If the next delivered offset is not exactly last_committed+1, the loop breaks immediately. Kafka offsets can legitimately skip: transaction markers, compacted topics, or messages dropped before submit. Example: offsets 100 and 102 are submitted, 101 never is. 100 commits, then start=101, 101 is not in all_offsets, the loop breaks, and 102 and everything after it can never be committed. The same happens on the first pass if a gap appears inside the tracked set. mark_committed only prunes offsets <= the committed one, so the set keeps growing, and nothing on a rebalance or revoke clears the tracker's state or its partition_locks.
findings.title: Commit permanently stalls on any non-contiguous offset gap

findings.consequence: On shutdown or rebalance, any item still queued is dropped. Its offset is never completed. The class docstring says no item is lost, but the pending results are silently discarded. Kafka will redeliver them only if the offsets were never committed.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and then calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), which is meant to let the worker drain the remaining items. But run() tests `while not self.shutdown` at the top of every iteration. After the item in progress finishes, the loop exits even though the queue still holds items. The drain never happens. The queue.ShutDown exception that would end the loop after a drain is never reached for those items. Python 3.13+ is the project's stated version (CLAUDE.md), so queue.ShutDown itself is available and is not a problem.
findings.title: Worker exits on the shutdown flag and leaves queued items unprocessed despite non-immediate queue shutdown

findings.consequence: A message whose processing failed is committed and never retried, so its result is silently lost.
findings.explanation: When result_processor raises, the exception is logged and swallowed. The finally block then calls complete_offset for that item anyway. The failed message's offset therefore counts as done and becomes committable. This contradicts the strategy docstring, which says offsets are committed only after successful processing. The same happens when queue.ShutDown interrupts processing and the loop breaks.
findings.title: Offset is marked complete in finally even when processing failed

findings.consequence: Under sustained load or a slow downstream, the backlog and the offset-tracking sets grow without limit. This can exhaust memory and OOM-kill the consumer, and the uncommitted work in memory is lost. Kafka's consumption rate is never throttled to the processing rate.
findings.explanation: FixedQueuePool creates each queue with `queue.Queue()` and no maxsize (line 185). FixedQueuePool.submit calls `work_queue.put(work_item)` (line 212), which never blocks or rejects. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit and poll() only record a gauge and apply no limit. Nothing bounds in-flight items, and the offset tracker's `all_offsets` and `outstanding` sets also grow with every submitted message. The class docstring says "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", but no code does that. When the Kafka consumer reads faster than the single worker per queue can process (slow result_processor, DB stalls), arroyo keeps feeding messages in.
findings.title: Unbounded queues: submit never applies backpressure despite docstring claiming it

findings.consequence: Every consumer restart or rebalance reprocesses the last message of each partition. For uptime results that means duplicate result processing. Partitions with offset gaps stop committing, so lag grows and the same messages are replayed after a restart.
findings.explanation: get_committable_offsets returns the highest contiguous processed offset N per partition. _commit_loop passes that value unchanged to commit_function (line 287). Arroyo and Kafka commit semantics treat a committed offset as the next offset to read, which is message.committable (offset+1). After a restart or rebalance, consumption therefore resumes at N, so message N is processed again. Separately, the contiguity scan stops at any offset missing from all_offsets. Compacted topics or transaction markers can leave such gaps, and a gap stalls commits for that partition permanently. mark_committed also prunes all_offsets, so a gap right after a commit is never bridged.
findings.title: Commit loop commits the last processed offset, not the next offset to consume

findings.consequence: After any partition rebalance, or any close and recreate of the strategy, the thread-queue-parallel consumer stops processing results. It still advances and commits offsets, so the messages are lost permanently. The loss is silent apart from log noise.
findings.explanation: The factory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes the same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy built in create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (line 255). Arroyo calls create_with_partitions on every rebalance and closes the old strategy. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() and terminate() call queue_pool.shutdown() (queue_consumer.py:335-342). That sets worker.shutdown and calls Queue.shutdown() on every queue, and the worker threads exit. The factory-owned pool is therefore dead after the first rebalance. The next strategy gets the same dead pool. In its submit(), queue.put raises ShutDown. The generic except at queue_consumer.py:317-325 catches it, then marks the offset added and completed. The commit loop then commits those offsets, so the messages are never processed. The OffsetTracker also keeps stale state across assignments.
findings.title: Shared queue pool is shut down by per-assignment strategy close, so later assignments silently drop and commit messages

findings.consequence: Concurrent commits can corrupt staged offsets or raise errors. During a rebalance, offsets for partitions that are no longer assigned can be committed, which can cause skipped or duplicated processing.
findings.explanation: commit_offsets (lines 249-252) is passed as commit_function to SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, which calls it from its own daemon commit thread (queue_consumer.py:287). Arroyo's Commit callable is meant to be called from the consumer's main thread. It stages and commits offsets on the non-thread-safe StreamProcessor/consumer state, and that state is also mutated by the main thread during poll, pause and rebalance. Calling it from another thread races with those operations.
findings.title: Kafka commit callback invoked from a background thread

findings.consequence: A regression that breaks per-group FIFO ordering in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy or FixedQueuePool would not be caught by this test. It gives false assurance for the ordering guarantee.
findings.explanation: The test's docstring says messages for the same subscription are processed in order. It submits five messages with offsets 100 to 104 for "sub1". It then asserts only that `len(self.processed_results) == 5`. Every result has the same payload, `{"subscription_id": "sub1", "data": "test"}`, so the results cannot be told apart by position. The test would still pass if the pool processed the items out of order.
findings.title: test_preserves_order_within_group never checks ordering

findings.consequence: The test cannot catch a regression where a failed message blocks commits. It asserts the opposite of the documented and implemented behavior, and it depends on racing the 1s commit-loop interval.
findings.explanation: The test's docstring says errors must not block offset commits. In the implementation, OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in a `finally` block even when the processor raises (queue_consumer.py:148-149). The offset tracker therefore treats offsets 100 (failed) and 101 (succeeded) as committable, and the commit loop would commit {partition: 102}. The test instead asserts at line 1922 that no commit exists for the partition. It only passes because the commit thread waits 1s before its first commit (queue_consumer.py:276), while the test's polling loop exits after about 0.3s. The assertion checks "not yet committed" rather than the behavior under test. The correct outcome is never checked. If processing or timing shifts, the test fails, since the real behavior is to commit.
findings.title: Error-handling test asserts no commit, contradicting its docstring and the real behavior; passes only on timing

findings.consequence: On Linux, rerunning the script leaves a stale webhook URL in .env while reporting success. Wrappers or CI that check the exit code cannot see tunnel startup failures.
findings.explanation: The script updates an existing GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with `sed -i '' -E ...`. That form only works with BSD/macOS sed. GNU sed on Linux treats `''` as an input file name, so the command fails and the .env file is not updated. The script then still prints the "✅ Updated GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL" message. Separately, `cleanup` always runs `exit 0`. The failure paths (rate limit hit, no tunnel URL extracted) call `cleanup`, so the script reports success when it failed.
findings.title: Webhook test script's `sed -i ''` is macOS-only and failures exit with status 0

findings.consequence: If a calendar service constructor throws, or deleteEvent fails, in the reschedule flow, the error is not logged and surfaces as an unhandled rejection. In serverless runtimes the deletion may also be cut off when the request returns, which leaves the old calendar event in place.
findings.explanation: The change turned the forEach callbacks into async functions so they can await getCalendar. forEach ignores the returned promises. In vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts (lines 125-137), the surrounding try/catch no longer catches anything from getCalendar or deleteEvent. Before, a synchronous throw from getCalendar (for example the CalendarService constructor) was caught and logged. Now it becomes an unhandled promise rejection. The same pattern is in bookings.tsx requestReschedule (lines ~553-570). There the code proceeds to send the reschedule emails and webhooks without waiting for the calendar deletions to finish, and a failed deletion is never handled.
findings.title: Async forEach callbacks make calendar/video deletion unawaited, escaping try/catch

findings.consequence: If a calendar or video deletion fails, nothing logs the error and the caller is not told. The old calendar or video event can stay in place while the reschedule is reported as successful. An unhandled rejection can also crash the Node process, depending on the runtime configuration.
findings.explanation: The change makes the forEach callback async by adding `await getCalendar(...)`. `forEach` ignores the promises the callback returns. The enclosing try/catch therefore cannot catch a rejection from getCalendar, deleteEvent or deleteMeeting. Those rejections become unhandled promise rejections. Nothing awaits the deletions. After the forEach, the function sends the reschedule email and returns true without waiting for them. The same code appears in packages/app-store/wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts and packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts. Before the change, getCalendar was called without await, and the code only returned the deleteEvent and deleteMeeting calls from the callback, which forEach also ignored. The change adds a new asynchronous failure path inside the callback, and the try/catch still does not cover it.
findings.title: Async forEach callbacks are not awaited, so deletion errors escape the try/catch

findings.consequence: An authenticated caller can send a malformed body and get an unhandled 500 instead of a 400 IncorrectBackupCode response. The impact is limited to the caller's own request.
findings.explanation: The new backup-code branch is taken for any truthy `req.body.backupCode`, then calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no type check. A JSON body like `{"backupCode": 123}` or `{"backupCode": {}}` passes the truthiness check, and `replaceAll` is not a function on those values, so the handler throws a TypeError. The same branch also calls `JSON.parse` on the decrypted codes without a guard. The password check for non-CAL identity providers is unchanged by this diff, so it is not a new defect. I found no rate limiting in this file.
findings.title: Non-string backupCode crashes the disable handler with an unhandled exception

findings.consequence: An attacker who holds only a backup code, which is a second-factor secret, can log in without knowing the password. That reduces two-factor authentication to a single factor. The same applies to accounts whose identity provider is not CAL.
findings.explanation: In authorize, the password is verified only when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode`. The new backup-code branch (`user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode`) is chosen independently of totpCode and never checks the TOTP value. A request to the credentials endpoint that sends any non-empty totpCode (for example "1") together with a valid backupCode skips password verification. It also skips the identityProvider guards, which are conditioned on `!credentials.totpCode`. The TOTP value is never validated on that path. The UI clears totpCode, but the API accepts both fields directly.
findings.title: Backup-code login can skip the password check when a junk totpCode is also sent

findings.consequence: When a caller omits `externalCalendarId` and the destination calendar is a non-primary calendar, the delete or cancel runs against the user's primary calendar. The event stays in the real destination calendar, or the wrong calendar is touched. Updates in the same situation fail because there is no calendarId.
findings.explanation: The old code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` when `externalCalendarId` was empty. The new fallback is `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That branch only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so it looks for a calendar whose externalId equals undefined, null or an empty string. That search never finds a real calendar and always returns undefined. In `deleteEvent` the call then uses the "primary" calendar instead of the event's destination calendar. In `updateEvent`, `calendarId` is undefined and the Google API call fails.
findings.title: Google deleteEvent/updateEvent lose the destination-calendar fallback

findings.consequence: Creating a booking with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar (for example, a user with no connected Google Calendar) now fails with a TypeError. Before this change it fell back to Cal Video, so the booking and its event creation break.
findings.explanation: destinationCalendar is now an array, and callers pass `[]` when neither the booking nor the user has a destination calendar. In `create`, `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` gives `undefined` for an empty or missing array. The next condition then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without optional chaining. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was null-safe. So when `evt.location === MeetLocationType` and there is no destination calendar, the property access throws instead of falling back to Cal Video (`integrations:daily`). The `&&` does not guard against this, because the left side is true in exactly that case. I did not read the callers of `create` in the snapshot. The three changed handlers (bookingReminder, confirm, editLocation) do build `[]` for this case.
findings.title: EventManager.create throws TypeError for Google Meet when destinationCalendar is empty

findings.consequence: The booking is not written to the other collective hosts' calendars. Nothing logs the omission.
findings.explanation: evt.destinationCalendar is null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar. The new code then runs `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`, and the optional chaining skips the push. Calendars collected from the other COLLECTIVE hosts (lines 992-993) are discarded. Example: a collective event where the organizer has no destination calendar but the second host has one. The team calendars are collected and never used.
findings.title: Collective team members' destination calendars silently dropped when organizer has none

findings.consequence: Calendar events created from Stripe or PayPal payment confirmation get an organizer attendee with id "undefined". PayPal events also lose the organizer's time format. Providers that validate the id may reject the event or store bad data.
findings.explanation: The Stripe getBooking, the cron reminder handler and the Stripe handlePaymentSuccess all build `organizer`, but only getBooking and the cron handler set `id`. handlePaymentSuccess in webhook.ts (organizer block, lines 219-225) and the PayPal handlePaymentSuccess (organizer block, lines 144-149) leave it out. The PayPal organizer also omits `timeFormat`. `Person.id` is optional in Calendar.d.ts, so this compiles. GoogleCalendarService spreads the organizer and sets `id: String(calEventRaw.organizer.id)` at lines 119 and 225. With no id that becomes the string "undefined" in the organizer attendee entry. These two handlers are the ones that create the calendar event after payment.
findings.title: Payment-success CalendarEvents omit organizer.id, which Google Calendar stringifies

findings.consequence: On instances without team billing, newly created organizations have a null slug. Org URL and subdomain routing break, and later slug-collision checks cannot match the org. On billing-enabled instances, the slug is claimed before payment or verification.
findings.explanation: The old code set `slug` when `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` and set `metadata.requestedSlug` only when billing was enabled. The change rewrote the first spread as `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}`, which drops the negation. With billing disabled, which is the self-hosted default, the organization is now created with neither `slug` nor `requestedSlug`. With billing enabled, `slug` is set immediately and `requestedSlug` is also set, so the organization is no longer pending approval of the requested slug. This is a behavior change inside a diff that otherwise only changes destinationCalendar to an array.
findings.title: Organization slug condition inverted: no slug is stored when team billing is disabled

findings.consequence: After a booking is cancelled or rescheduled, reminder rows may stay uncancelled and the scheduled SMS or email may still be sent to attendees for a cancelled booking. Failures are also invisible to the request.
findings.explanation: deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async. They call Twilio or SendGrid and then run Prisma update/delete calls, and they swallow their own errors. The old code started the provider cancel without awaiting it, but it put the DB deleteMany calls in prismaPromises, so Promise.all awaited them before the response. The new loop in handleCancelBooking.ts calls the async functions without awaiting or collecting their promises. The same applies to the new reschedule loop in handleNewBooking.ts. In a serverless handler, the response can be returned, and the runtime frozen, before these calls finish.
findings.title: Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget, no longer awaited with the other cancel work

findings.consequence: Cancelled or rescheduled bookings whose reminders are already scheduled at SendGrid may not get their batches cancelled. Their emails are then still sent. Stale cancelled rows also pile up. I did not confirm that the booking-cancel path sets cancelled=true on unscheduled reminders.
findings.explanation: The hypothesis about the earlier deleteMany is not the real problem. A reminder with scheduledDate <= now has already fired, so deleting it without a cancel is harmless. The real defect is in the new cancel block. It selects every cancelled reminder due within the hour, with no filter on method, scheduled or referenceId. WorkflowReminder.referenceId is nullable (schema.prisma:640). A cancelled reminder that was never sent to SendGrid has a null referenceId, so batch_id is null and the request throws. The single try/catch wraps the whole for loop, so the first throw skips all remaining reminders. The delete promises are lazy and only run in Promise.all after the loop, so none of the deletes run either. The failing row is never deleted, so the same row fails on every cron run and blocks all later cancellations.
findings.title: Cancel loop aborts on first failing SendGrid call, e.g. a reminder with null referenceId

findings.consequence: A zero-length override is not treated as blocking through this branch. It relies on the later isBefore/isSame/isAfter checks, which may not cover the case.
findings.explanation: `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created objects with `===`, so it is always false. The intended zero-length override (day marked unavailable) case is never handled by this branch.
findings.title: Object identity comparison of dayjs instances in date-override check never matches

findings.consequence: Valid slots disappear from getSchedule for hosts with more than one availability range on a day. Slots that end after closing time are still offered, because the end bound is never checked against the slot end.
findings.explanation: In checkIfIsAvailable, `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` (the same expression as `start`), not from `slotEndTime`. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past `endTime` is therefore never rejected. The check also uses `workingHours.find(...)` and returns 'outside' as soon as any single entry for that weekday fails `start < startTime || end > endTime`. A day with split availability, such as 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, produces two entries. A 14:00 slot is outside the first entry (`end > 720`), so `find` matches and the function returns false. The slot is dropped even though it lies inside the second range. The same split-range problem affects overlapping or multi-range availability for any user.
findings.title: Working-hours check uses slot start as slot end and rejects slots when a day has several working-hour ranges

findings.consequence: Timing comparison of the secret is only a minor risk over a network. Malformed webhook payloads produce 500 responses with unhandled exceptions rather than clean 400s.
findings.explanation: The auth bypass in the hypothesis does not happen. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is defined in packages/lib/constants.ts:103 as CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY. The handler returns 403 at line 19 unless both are non-empty. So an unset secret cannot match a missing header, and the `|| ""` key fallback at line 56 cannot be reached with an empty key. Two weaker defects remain. (1) The secret check at lines 24-27 uses `!==`, which is not constant-time, so response timing can leak the secret. (2) `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` (line 30) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (lines 55-57) are not wrapped in try/catch. A malformed body, a bad ciphertext or invalid JSON throws, and the caller gets a 500 instead of a 400.
findings.title: Webhook secret compared with !== (not constant-time); parse and decrypt errors are unhandled

findings.consequence: A non-admin team member can install or overwrite team-level app credentials, such as calendar or video integrations, which the code intends to restrict to team admins. Malformed state values also cause a 500 instead of a 4xx.
findings.explanation: createOAuthAppCredential takes teamId from the unsigned JSON in req.query.state. When state.teamId is set, it only checks that the session user is an accepted member of that team (lines 30-45). It then creates a team credential and returns (lines 47-56). throwIfNotHaveAdminAccessToTeam is called only after that branch, at line 59. By then state.teamId is falsy, so the call is always passed null and returns immediately. The admin check is therefore dead code. A plain team member can set state={"teamId":N} on the OAuth callback and create a credential for that team. The state has no signature, nonce or session binding, so it can be forged or replayed (decodeOAuthState.ts, encodeOAuthState.ts). JSON.parse in decodeOAuthState is unguarded, so malformed state throws and gives a 500.
findings.title: Team credential created for any accepted member using unsigned, client-controlled state.teamId; admin check is never applied

findings.consequence: With credential sync enabled, a refresh overwrites the stored refresh_token with the string "refresh_token" and the expiry becomes NaN. The next refresh then fails, so users' Zoom connections and the other synced apps break and need re-authorization.
findings.explanation: In minimumTokenResponseSchema, `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` are ordinary computed keys. Zod schema instances don't override toString, so both evaluate to "[object Object]". The second entry overwrites the first, which leaves the schema as { access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown optional }. These are not wildcard keys, and the "any numeric property is the expiry" intent is not implemented. The hypothesis expected a required "ZodString" key and a parse failure, but that is not what happens. Any response with an access_token parses successfully. Zod's default object mode then strips every other field, including expires_in, expiry_date and the real refresh_token. parseRefreshTokenResponse then sets refresh_token to the literal "refresh_token" on the stripped data. Zoom's caller (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:111-124) takes data.refresh_tok…
findings.title: Computed schema keys collapse to "[object Object]", so the token response is stripped and the placeholder refresh_token is saved

findings.consequence: With APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and a sync endpoint configured, Google Calendar token refresh always fails. The failure is swallowed and the expired access token keeps being used, so calendar calls fail. Error responses from the sync endpoint are not detected.
findings.explanation: When credential sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the fetch Response from the sync endpoint. It does not check the status and does not parse the body. The Google caller reads `res?.data`, which is an axios/googleapis shape. A fetch Response has no `.data`, so `token` is undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The surrounding catch only handles the `invalid_grant` message. Any other error returns `myGoogleAuth` silently, so the token is never refreshed from the sync endpoint and the credential is not updated. The Google caller also passes `googleCredentials`, not the refreshed response, to parseRefreshTokenResponse. A successful sync-endpoint response would therefore never be validated or persisted. The two branches of refreshOAuthTokens return different shapes. The refresh-function branch returns googleapis `res`, which has `.data`. The sync branch returns a…
findings.title: Sync-endpoint branch returns a raw fetch Response, which Google's refresh path reads as axios-style `.data`

findings.consequence: After the first successful token refresh, the user's Google Calendar credential is corrupted in the database. Every later Google Calendar operation for that credential throws a parse error until the user reconnects.
findings.explanation: The change replaced `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)`, which returned the parsed credential, with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)`. That helper returns the zod `safeParse` result, `{ success, data }`. The result is assigned to `key` and written with `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored credential key becomes `{ success: true, data: {...} }`. The next read through `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` at the top of `googleAuth` fails because `access_token`, `refresh_token` and the other fields are missing at the top level.
findings.title: Google refresh stores the safeParse wrapper object instead of the credential key

findings.consequence: Constructing `SalesforceCalendarService` rejects on every call, so Salesforce integration is broken. If the missing import were added, the connection would still use the expired token.
findings.explanation: The new refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update` at line 96. The grep for `prisma` in this file finds only that line, so there is no import of `@calcom/prisma`. Running `getClient` therefore throws a ReferenceError. Separately, the refreshed token is never used. The `jsforce.Connection` at line 106 is still built with `credentialKey.access_token`, the old token, instead of `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.
findings.title: Salesforce getClient uses prisma without importing it and builds the connection with the stale access token

findings.consequence: Permanently unsendable SMS reminders are re-fetched and re-processed, including extra DB lookups, on every cron run for up to 7 days until their scheduled date passes. The new retry limit does not bound them.
findings.explanation: The retry increment was added only for the case where twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy or throws. When `message?.length && sendTo` is false, for example when sendTo or smsReminderNumber is null or the template yields no message, the code does nothing: it doesn't set scheduled, doesn't increment retryCount, and doesn't delete the reminder. Such a reminder matches the `scheduled: false` query on every cron run. It is only removed once scheduledDate passes, via the first deleteMany branch. The new `retryCount > 1` cleanup never applies to it. The cleanup also runs at `gt: 1`, so a reminder is deleted after 2 failed attempts, not 3. The new `retryCount > 1` OR branch also has no `method: SMS` filter, so it would delete reminders of any method once their count exceeds 1. Only the SMS path increments retryCount today, so this is latent.
findings.title: Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo never get retryCount incremented

findings.consequence: One failing or missing reminder can make the cron return a 500 and leave the other pending SMS reminders unscheduled until the next run.
findings.explanation: The new catch block calls prisma.workflowReminder.update to bump retryCount without its own try/catch. If that update throws, the error escapes the for-loop and the handler. This can happen if the row no longer exists (P2025, for example when it was deleted concurrently) or if the database is failing. The failure that brought the code into the catch block is then lost, and all remaining reminders in the batch are skipped for this run. The migration and schema change are compatible: the column is NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, so existing rows are fine. The new delete clause `retryCount > 1` has no `method: SMS` filter. Today only this handler writes retryCount, so that is latent.
findings.title: Unguarded retryCount update in catch block can abort the whole batch

prs.title: SMS workflow reminder retry count tracking

findings.consequence: Team admins and owners cannot add guests to team members' bookings, even though the code intends to allow it. They get a FORBIDDEN error.
findings.explanation: The handler computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner` as `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. The name and intent are "admin OR owner", but `&&` makes the check true only when the user passes both tests. A team admin who is not the owner, or an owner whose membership is not counted as admin, fails this check. Such a user is rejected with FORBIDDEN unless they are also the organizer or an attendee. When `eventType.teamId` is missing, `?? 0` makes both lookups use team id 0. I did not read `isTeamAdmin` or `isTeamOwner` to confirm their exact semantics.
findings.title: Team admin/owner permission check uses && so it requires both roles

findings.consequence: The blacklist and existing-attendee checks can be bypassed with mixed-case emails. Duplicate attendee rows and duplicate emails can be created. Large guest lists can be used to spam outbound email.
findings.explanation: The schema at line 5 is only z.array(z.string().email()). It has no toLowerCase, trim, dedupe or .max(). addGuests.handler.ts:74-78 compares guests to attendee.email and to the lowercased blacklist with exact string equality. An input such as "Blocked@X.com" therefore passes a blacklist entry "blocked@x.com". "Existing@x.com" passes the check against an existing attendee "existing@x.com". The input ["a@x.com","a@x.com"] passes the filter and goes to createMany at line 102 with duplicate rows. The handler does no normalization of its own. The array has no size limit, so a request can add and email an unbounded number of guests. The handler also sends emails to the raw `guests` (line 168) rather than `uniqueGuests`.
findings.title: guests schema does not normalize, dedupe or bound emails

prs.title: Add guest management functionality to existing bookings

findings.consequence: When the device limit is reached, a legitimate already-registered anonymous device that sends a repeat request with unchanged values can be rejected with a limit error. Authenticate then fails for a user who should be allowed. The window is narrow, so the impact is limited.
findings.explanation: updateDevice maps every result with rowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. A zero count does not mean the device is missing. go-sql-driver/mysql returns changed rows rather than matched rows unless clientFoundRows is set. An existing device in the window whose client_ip, user_agent and updated_at all equal the stored values therefore reports 0. findings.consequence: A user who is allowed to access resource X can be wrongly denied for up to the short cache TTL. This happens after a different resource Y, whose name and parent concatenate to the same string, was denied. The result is intermittent, hard-to-diagnose 403s.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the key as namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent. The fields are joined with '_', which can appear in Grafana resource names, folder UIDs and user UIDs. Two different checks can therefore produce the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="c" and name="a" with parent="b_c" both give "..._a_b_c". When one check is denied, Check stores the key in permDenialCache. Check consults that cache first and returns Allowed=false for the other check without evaluating permissions. This is a fail-closed false denial, not an access grant. The key also shares the ".perm_<uid>_<action>" prefix with the permission-map key, which makes collisions and confusion easier.
findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because name and parent are joined with '_'

findings.consequence: A user can be wrongly denied access to a resource they are allowed to see. This lasts until the cache TTL expires. The wrong result has no fallback and is hard to diagnose. Someone who can pick resource names or folder UIDs could also trigger denials for other resources.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey builds namespace.perm_<uid>_<action>_<name>_<parent> with a plain '_' separator. A name or parent that contains '_' can produce the same key as a different pair. For example, name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both give "..._a_b_c". Grafana UIDs and resource names can contain '_'. An empty name or parent shifts the fields in the same way. Check() returns Allowed=false straight from permDenialCache.Get on a key hit, before any permission evaluation. The wrapped caches share one underlying cache and the key has no type prefix. Because of that, a denial cached for one resource also denies a different resource that maps to the same key.
findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous because it joins fields with unescaped '_'

findings.consequence: After a cold start, a burst of page renders does redundant manifest reads and parses, one after another. In Dev mode, every request that needs web assets queues behind the exclusive lock. The impact is limited to latency.
findings.explanation: GetWebAssets reads the cache under RLock and returns early if it is set (outside Dev). On a miss it takes the exclusive Lock and goes straight to reading and parsing the manifest. It never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock. If N requests arrive while the cache is cold, all N see nil. Each one then takes the lock in turn and re-reads the manifest from disk, even though the first has already filled the cache. In Dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed, so every request takes the exclusive lock and does file I/O. The old code also re-read the manifest on every Dev request, so that behavior is not new. The new lock now serializes those reads. The returned pointer is only replaced, never mutated in place, so there is no data race.

findings.consequence: A crafted ECDSA signature with an empty INTEGER makes verification fail with an unchecked exception instead of the expected IOException or a clean invalid-signature result. This can bypass callers' error handling.
findings.explanation: readInteger passes the content bytes to new BigInteger(bytes) with no check that length > 0. A signature such as 30 04 02 00 02 00 passes readSequence (two elements, each [02 00]). readInteger then reads length 0 and calls new BigInteger(new byte[0]), which throws NumberFormatException ("Zero length BigInteger"). It does not throw IOException. The caller asn1derToConcatenatedRS declares only IOException and does not catch runtime exceptions. Other malformed input, such as truncated or oversized lengths, does produce IOException. The tag and length arithmetic in readNext (mark, count, reset) is correct for 1-byte and 2-byte lengths and for a leading 0x00 in r or s. Indefinite lengths cannot reach new byte[-1], because readNext returns only the tag byte for them and readInteger then hits EOF.
findings.title: readInteger throws unchecked NumberFormatException on zero-length INTEGER

findings.consequence: Malformed or non-canonical ECDSA signatures can be accepted. Short input produces an unexpected runtime exception. The impact is limited because this is a minimal client-side provider.
findings.explanation: In asn1derToConcatenatedRS, integerToBytes drops the high-order bytes when the BigInteger's byte array is longer than qLength. A DER signature whose r or s is larger than the curve order size is not rejected. Its low len bytes are used instead, so the check passes on a different value. A DER signature with extra high bytes therefore verifies as if it were the canonical one, which makes the signature malleable. Negative DER integers are also accepted, because their two's-complement bytes are copied. concatenatedRSToASN1DER also does not check that signature.length is at least signLength. A short input throws an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from System.arraycopy instead of an IOException. Lines 114-115 build two ASN1Encoder results and discard them. The ES512 sizes are correct: signLength is 132, len is 66, and the len+1 buffer with a leading zero gives non-negative values.
findings.title: integerToBytes silently truncates oversized r/s; redundant encoder calls

findings.consequence: The emoji resize job fails with ArgumentError, so emoji are not downsized. Only the new "80%" call in the uploads controller works.
findings.explanation: Ruby has no method overloading. `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` at line 149 replaces `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145. The existing caller in app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`. That call now binds dimensions=100 and opts=100, and the fifth argument raises ArgumentError because the method accepts at most four. A four-argument call such as `downsize(from, to, 100, 100)` would bind opts=100, and `opts[:allow_animation]` would then raise a TypeError. Either way, the width/height form no longer works.
findings.title: Second `downsize` definition overwrites the width/height version, breaking existing callers

prs.title: FEATURE: automatically downsize large images

findings.consequence: A user who follows the unsubscribe link without a TopicUser row gets a 500 error and is not unsubscribed. The action also changes state on a GET request.
findings.explanation: The new `unsubscribe` action looks up the row with `TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` and then immediately calls `tu.notification_level`. `find_by` returns nil when the user has no TopicUser row for that topic. This can happen if the user opens an unsubscribe link from an old email, was never tracked on the topic, or the row was removed. In that case the call raises NoMethodError.
findings.title: unsubscribe action dereferences a possibly nil TopicUser

prs.title: FEATURE: per-topic unsubscribe option in emails

findings.consequence: Anyone who wants to use a blocked email address can sign up by changing the case of any letter, which defeats the feature.
findings.explanation: BlockedEmail.should_block? looks the address up with an exact-match `where(email: email)`. The User model does not lowercase emails before validation or save. A search of user.rb finds only `Email.downcase` in the login lookup and a downcase for the avatar hash. If `spam@example.com` is on the block list, a signup with `Spam@Example.com` finds no record. should_block? then returns nil and the address passes validation. Mail still reaches the same mailbox.
findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive, so a blocked address can be bypassed by changing case

prs.title: Add comprehensive email validation for blocked users

findings.consequence: A re-run or a migration-version mismatch silently destroys the stored embed mappings.
findings.explanation: The CreateTopicEmbeds migration uses `force: true`. If the migration runs against a database where `topic_embeds` already exists, it drops that table and all its rows before recreating it. The same pattern was added to the existing CreateTopTopics migration.
findings.title: create_table with force: true drops an existing topic_embeds table

findings.consequence: Running the Disqus import produces topics with wrong creation dates and no category placement. Existing scripts that pass `-c` lose their category with no warning, and the import can abort partway when a source page is not fetchable.
findings.explanation: The change removes the `--category` option and replaces PostCreator with `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`. That call accepts only a title. `t[:created_at]` is no longer passed, so imported topics are dated at import time instead of the Disqus thread date. The category lookup is gone, so every imported topic lands in the default category. `import_remote` also fetches `t[:link]` over HTTP, so an unreachable article URL raises mid-import. It also needs the new `ruby-readability` gem.
findings.title: Disqus import drops original thread date and the category option

findings.consequence: Removing the feed_polling_url or embed_by_username guard from Jobs::PollFeed#execute would not make any spec fail. A blank URL or username could then reach poll_feed unnoticed.
findings.explanation: The "requires feed_polling_url" and "requires embed_by_username" examples stub only one setting. feed_polling_enabled defaults to false in config/site_settings.yml:355, and neither example stubs it to true. The first condition in execute (app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:15) is therefore false, and poll_feed is never called. That holds even if the url or username checks were removed from execute, so the examples do not test what they claim.
findings.title: PollFeed specs for feed_polling_url and embed_by_username cannot fail

The button used to sit at the right edge of the row. Now it is a normal flex item placed directly after .small-action-desc. The desc has no flex-grow and the button has no margin-left:auto.

findings.consequence: Users with no website get `website_name: null` in the JSON. The intended omission of the key does not happen. The template's `{{#if model.website_name}}` hides the nil value, so the UI is unaffected. The impact is limited to extra payload and dead code.
findings.explanation: ActiveModel::Serializer only calls conditional-include hooks named include_<attr>?. The change defines `include_website_name` with no `?`, so the serializer never calls it. The same file uses the correct form for `include_email?` and `include_card_image_badge_id?`. As a result `website_name` is always serialized, including when the user has no website. The guard `website.present?` has no effect.
findings.title: include_website_name is missing the trailing ? so it is never called

For `.topic-meta-data h5 a`, the original light color was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The new code uses `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 70%)` as the light branch. Every other converted rule keeps its original light value, so this one looks like a copy-paste error. The author link in the "in reply to" expansion becomes much lighter in the default light theme.

findings.consequence: On light themes, group member names become noticeably lighter and lower in contrast. They are no longer visually distinct from the titles. This is a visual regression on both desktop and mobile.
findings.explanation: The other edits in this change wrap the existing light-theme colour in dark-light-choose and add a dark-theme variant. The `.group-member-info .name` rule was different. Its original colour was `scale-color($primary, $lightness: 30%)`. The change replaced it with `dark-light-choose(scale-color($primary, $lightness: 50%), scale-color($secondary, $lightness: 50%))`. findings.consequence: For groups whose member count is an exact multiple of the page size, the admin UI offers a next page that is always empty. The last real page is never marked as last.
findings.explanation: totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1. When user_count is an exact multiple of limit (for example 50 members with limit 50), it returns 2 instead of 1. currentPage is 1 at offset 0, so showingLast (currentPage == totalPages) is false. The "next" action then sets offset to min(0+50, 50) = 50 and calls findMembers, which loads an empty page. The same off-by-one affects every exact-multiple count (100, 150, and so on).
findings.title: totalPages over-counts by one when user_count is a multiple of limit

findings.consequence: Anyone can make the endpoint return a 500 with a negative limit or offset. Anyone can also force the server to load and serialize an entire large group in one request, which defeats the pagination this change adds.
findings.explanation: GroupsController#members, which any user who can see the group can call, converts params[:limit] and params[:offset] with to_i and passes them straight to limit() and offset(). Nothing clamps them. A negative limit, such as limit=-1, produces an invalid SQL LIMIT on PostgreSQL, so the request fails with a 500. A very large limit, such as limit=1000000, loads and serializes every member of the group in one request. The old code applied limit/offset only to automatic groups. This change makes every group go through this path, and the new meta block echoes the raw values back to the client.
findings.title: members endpoint accepts unvalidated limit/offset from a public request

prs.title: FIX: proper handling of group memberships

findings.consequence: After the site default locale is changed, users whose locale lacks a translation can keep getting strings in the previous default language until the cache is reset or the process restarts. Lookups outside controller requests can also fall through to the key or a "translation missing" string.
findings.explanation: The fallback chain is now [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale, :en], so it depends on a site setting that admins can change at runtime. The LRU cache key in translate is only "#{key}#{config.locale}#{backend.object_id}". Take a locale such as fr whose translation for a key is missing. Its fallback result is cached under the key for fr. If the admin then changes default_locale, the cache entry still holds the value resolved from the old default locale. The cache is not cleared on that change, and reload! is the only thing that resets it. In addition, translate loads only config.locale and never the fallback locales. Callers outside set_locale, such as jobs and mailers using I18n.with_locale, never call ensure_loaded!, so their fallback lookups can resolve to a locale that is not loaded.
findings.title: Translation cache key ignores the dynamic site-default fallback locale

prs.title: FEATURE: Localization fallbacks (server-side)

findings.consequence: With `__rest_serializer` payloads, a missing sub-object produces `[undefined, ...]`, which breaks consumers that iterate the list. Unrelated `*_ids` fields lose their raw values. A null `*_ids` value throws during hydration.
findings.explanation: In the `_ids` branch, each id goes through `_lookupSubType`. That returns undefined when the root collection is absent or the id is missing, and for `category` when `findById` misses. The result array then holds undefined entries. `hydrated || []` is dead code because an array is always truthy. `delete obj[k]` runs unconditionally. The singular branch keeps the raw `*_id` when lookup fails, so the two branches disagree. After a failed lookup the original id array is gone and cannot be recovered. The regex now also matches any embedded object's key ending in `_ids`, such as a plain array of numeric ids with no matching root collection. That key is rewritten to a pluralized property full of undefined. `obj[k].map` also throws if the value is null or not an array.
findings.title: Plural *_ids hydration yields undefined entries and unconditionally deletes the raw ids

findings.consequence: A stale admin tab or a double delete returns a 500 instead of a 404.
findings.explanation: `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` returns nil for an unknown or already-deleted id. `update` passes that nil to `save_host`, which calls `host.host=` on it. `destroy` calls `host.destroy` on it directly. Both raise NoMethodError.
findings.title: update/destroy dereference a nil host when the id does not exist

findings.consequence: An embedding request whose host differs in case from the stored entry is wrongly rejected.
findings.explanation: `record_for_host` runs `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` with `uri.host`. It does not downcase `uri.host`. `URI(...).host` keeps the case it was given, so a request from `Example.com` is compared against the lowercased column and never matches.
findings.title: Host lookup compares lower(host) against a non-downcased value

findings.consequence: `rake db:migrate` aborts with NoMethodError on installs that never customized `embed_category`, which is most of them. The upgrade then cannot complete, and the old `embeddable_hosts` setting is never moved into the new table.
findings.explanation: The migration reads `execute(...)[0]['id']` from a query that joins categories to the `embed_category` site setting. Discourse stores a setting only after it has been changed from its default. On a site that never set `embed_category`, the query returns no rows, so `[0]` is nil and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError. The fallback lookup of `uncategorized_category_id` has the same problem: `[0]['value']` fails if that row is absent. The migration also uses `create_table force: true`, which drops any existing table. It builds INSERT statements by interpolating the raw `embeddable_hosts` lines with `'#{h}'`, so a value containing a quote breaks the SQL.
findings.title: Migration crashes when embed_category or uncategorized_category_id has no site_settings row
